text: Rice quality and quantity losses build up at every step between cutting the crop and eating or selling it — not only in the field. A regional estimate cited in the source (from Cambodia's General Directorate of Agriculture, June 2011) breaks total postharvest loss down by stage as illustrative minimum-to-maximum ranges rather than fixed numbers: harvesting/cutting (ច្រូតកាត់) about 1-3%; field handling and stacking of bundled rice (លើកដាក់) about 2-7%; threshing (បោកបែន) about 2-6%; drying (សម្ងួត) about 1-5%; storage (ទុកដាក់) about 2-6%; and transport (ដឹកជញ្ជូន) about 2-10%. Added together, total postharvest loss for the region is commonly put at roughly 10% to 37% of the harvested crop, though the real number for any one farm depends on how carefully each step is handled. In developing countries generally, postharvest paddy loss is often quoted around 10-15% under reasonable management, but can run much higher — toward 50% of potential value — where harvesting is delayed, weather is bad, or storage is poor. In more mechanized farming systems (parts of Europe and North America are mentioned as examples), losses are typically much lower, often cited around 5%. Because the loss happens gradually across many small steps rather than one dramatic event, tightening up several stages together (harvesting on time, threshing promptly, drying properly, storing dry and clean, handling transport carefully) usually gives the biggest overall improvement, rather than fixing only one stage. (Note: these percentage ranges are regional averages given for illustration in the source; treat them as a general guide rather than a precise measurement for your own field, and expect real losses to vary by season, variety, and equipment.)
